items.title: The hardest natural material and pencil 'lead' are the same element
items.claim: Diamond scores 10 on the Mohs scale, the maximum. Graphite scores 1-2 — it streaks on paper. Both are 100 percent pure carbon. Identical atoms, opposite mechanical properties.

options.text: Diamond contains stronger isotopes of carbon
Diamond's sp3 carbons form a rigid 3D tetrahedral lattice (all sigma bonds); graphite's sp2 carbons form strong hexagonal sheets held together only by weak dispersion forces, so sheets slide
Diamond is at higher temperature when it forms

items.reveal:
Diamond: every carbon bonded tetrahedrally to four others, all strong sigma bonds. No mobile electrons (insulator), no slip planes (hard).

Graphite: each carbon sp2-hybridised, three in-plane sigma bonds plus a delocalised pi system across the sheet. Sheets stack 0.335 nm apart, held only by van der Waals forces. The pi electrons conduct along the layers; the layers slide past each other — hence the pencil streak.

Thermodynamically, graphite is more stable than diamond by 2.9 kJ/mol at room temperature and pressure. Diamond is metastable; only a kinetic barrier stops it converting to graphite over geological time.
items.why: Element identity isn't enough — bonding arrangement (allotropy) can transform a substance utterly.

items.title: Push CO2 hard enough and it becomes neither gas nor liquid
items.claim: Above 31.1°C and 73.8 bar, carbon dioxide enters a 'supercritical' state — it fills its container like a gas but has the density and solvent power of a liquid. It is now the standard solvent for decaffeinating coffee.
items.prompt: Why is supercritical CO2 useful for extracting compounds from natural materials?

options.text: It penetrates porous solids like a gas, dissolves organics like a liquid, and can be removed cleanly by depressurisation — leaving no solvent residue
It is the only solvent that dissolves caffeine

items.reveal:
On a pressure-temperature phase diagram, the liquid-gas boundary terminates at a critical point. Beyond it, the distinction between liquid and gas disappears — there is a single fluid phase whose density can be tuned continuously by changing pressure.

For CO2 the critical point is at 31.1°C and 73.8 bar — easily reachable in industrial equipment. Supercritical CO2 dissolves caffeine but not the flavour compounds in coffee beans. After extraction, depressurising vaporises the CO2 instantly with no residue.

Applications: hop extraction for beer, essential oil isolation, dry cleaning, semiconductor cleaning, dyeing textiles without water, and recently as a working fluid in highly efficient power-cycle generators.
items.why: Phase diagrams in GCSE end at the liquid-gas boundary. The fluid beyond the critical point has properties of both — and quietly underpins major industries.
